relearning.title: Read: building and reading a karyotype
relearning.description: A short reading with the sock-sorting analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can design a karyotype to demonstrate inheritance patterns.**

**Think of matching socks from the laundry.** You dump out the pile, find each sock's partner by size and pattern, and line the pairs up from biggest to smallest. Now you can quickly see if a sock is missing or if there is an extra. A **karyotype** is the same thing for chromosomes: a picture of a cell's chromosomes sorted into pairs.

**How to build a karyotype:**
1. Pair each chromosome with its homolog. Match them by **size**, **centromere position** and **banding pattern** (the stripes).
2. Arrange the pairs from **largest (1) to smallest (22)**. These 22 pairs are the **autosomes**.
3. Put the **sex chromosomes** (pair 23) last: **XX = female**, **XY = male**.
4. Count. A typical human karyotype has **46 chromosomes in 23 pairs**.

**Worked example:** A karyotype shows 22 matched pairs of autosomes, plus one X and one Y. Total = 44 + 2 = 46. This is a typical male.

checks.explanation: Pairs 1–22 are autosomes. Only pair 23 (XX or XY) is the sex chromosomes, which is the common mix-up.

checks.prompt: A karyotype has 46 chromosomes, and pair 23 is XX. What does it show?

options.text: A female with an extra chromosome

checks.explanation: 46 is the typical number, and XX means female. A male would have XY, and an extra chromosome would make 47.

sections.title: Spotting changes and following inheritance

body.text:
**Nondisjunction:** chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis, so a gamete gets an extra copy or is missing one. On a karyotype it shows up as a set of three or a single.

**Trisomy** = three copies of one chromosome (47 total). **Monosomy** = only one copy (45 total).

**Examples:**
**Down syndrome:** trisomy 21 (three copies of chromosome 21), 47 chromosomes.
**Klinefelter syndrome:** XXY, 47 chromosomes, male.
**Turner syndrome:** a single X (written XO), 45 chromosomes, female.

**Worked example 2:** A karyotype shows three copies of chromosome 21, and pair 23 is XX. Total = 47. This is a female with Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

**How sex is inherited:** a mother can only give an X. A father gives either an X or a Y. The Punnett square for XX × XY:

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & \mathrm{X} & \mathrm{X} \\ \hline \mathrm{X} & \mathrm{XX} & \mathrm{XX} \\ \mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{XY} & \mathrm{XY} \end{array}$$

2 boxes are XX and 2 are XY, so every child has a **50% chance** of being a boy. The father's sperm decides.

**Worked example 3:** An egg with 24 chromosomes (two copies of 21) is fertilized by a normal sperm (23). The zygote has 24 + 23 = 47, with three copies of chromosome 21.

**Watch out for:** counting pairs instead of chromosomes (23 pairs = 46 chromosomes), calling the sex chromosomes autosomes, thinking a trisomy means 3 extra chromosomes (it is one extra, making three copies), and forgetting to check pair 23 for the sex.

checks.prompt: A karyotype shows trisomy 18. How many chromosomes does it have in total? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Trisomy is one extra chromosome: 46 + 1 = 47. Adding 3 (to get 49) is the common mistake; three copies means just one extra.

checks.prompt: Which parent's gamete decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl?
checks.explanation: Every egg carries an X. A sperm carries either an X (girl) or a Y (boy), so the father's sperm decides.

sections.shortAnswer: A karyotype has 47 chromosomes, and pair 23 is XXY. Describe this person and explain how nondisjunction could have caused it.

relearning.title: Do: read a karyotype, then trace nondisjunction
relearning.description: Two worked problems shown one step at a time: reading a karyotype, then predicting karyotypes after nondisjunction.

body.problem: A student builds a karyotype from a photo of chromosomes. Pairs 1–20 and pair 22 each have 2 chromosomes. Chromosome 21 has 3. Pair 23 is an X and a Y. Describe the karyotype.

steps.text: **Sort:** pair the chromosomes by size, centromere position and banding pattern. Line the pairs up from 1 (largest) to 22 (smallest), with the sex chromosomes last.
**Count:** 21 autosome pairs with 2 each = 42. Chromosome 21 has 3. The sex chromosomes add 2. Total = 42 + 3 + 2 = 47.
**Sex:** pair 23 is XY, so this is a male.
**Abnormality:** three copies of chromosome 21 is trisomy 21.
**Conclusion:** 47 chromosomes, XY, trisomy 21: a male with Down syndrome.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a karyotype has 2 copies of every autosome (pairs 1–22) and only one X, with no second sex chromosome. How many chromosomes are there in total? Type a number.
checks.explanation: 22 pairs × 2 = 44 autosomes, plus 1 X = 45. Answering 46 means counting a second sex chromosome that isn't there.

checks.prompt: What does that karyotype (45 chromosomes, a single X) show?
checks.explanation: A single X with 45 chromosomes is Turner syndrome, and the person is female. Klinefelter is XXY (47, male), and Down syndrome is trisomy 21.

body.problem: During meiosis in a mother, the two X chromosomes fail to separate (nondisjunction). One egg gets both X's and another egg gets no X. Each egg is fertilized by a normal sperm carrying an X or a Y. Predict the karyotypes.

steps.text: **Normal gametes:** an egg has 22 autosomes + X = 23. A sperm has 22 autosomes + X or Y = 23.
**The unusual eggs:** the XX egg has 22 + 2 = 24 chromosomes. The egg with no X has 22.
**XX egg:** + X sperm → XXX, 47 chromosomes (a female with an extra X). + Y sperm → XXY, 47 chromosomes: Klinefelter syndrome, male.
**No-X egg:** + X sperm → a single X, 45 chromosomes: Turner syndrome, female. + Y sperm → Y only, which can't survive, because every person needs at least one X.
**On the karyotypes:** each child's change shows at pair 23, and the count tells you trisomy (47) or monosomy (45).

checks.prompt: Your turn: an egg is missing chromosome 21 because of nondisjunction. How many chromosomes does it have? Type a number.
checks.explanation: A normal egg has 23. Missing one leaves 23 − 1 = 22. Starting from 46 is the common mistake, since an egg is haploid.

checks.prompt: An XX egg (from nondisjunction) is fertilized by a Y sperm. What karyotype results?
checks.explanation: 24 + 23 = 47, and the sex chromosomes are XXY: Klinefelter syndrome. A Y means male even with two X's, which is the common trap.

checks.prompt: A typical human karyotype has 23 pairs of chromosomes. How many chromosomes is that in all? Type a number.
checks.explanation: 23 pairs × 2 = 46 chromosomes. Counting pairs instead of chromosomes (answering 23) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: When you build a karyotype, how do you find each chromosome's partner?

options.text: Pair up any two chromosomes that are next to each other
Pair each autosome with a sex chromosome
Match them by size, centromere position and banding pattern

checks.explanation: Homologs match in size, centromere position and banding pattern (the stripes). Then the pairs are lined up from largest (1) to smallest (22), with the sex chromosomes last.

sections.title: Reading Karyotypes

checks.prompt: A karyotype has 45 chromosomes because one chromosome has only one copy instead of two. What is this called?
checks.explanation: Monosomy means only one copy, for 45 total. Trisomy is three copies of one chromosome, for 47 total.

checks.prompt: A karyotype shows three copies of chromosome 21, and pair 23 is XX. What does it show?
checks.explanation: Three copies of chromosome 21 is trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), and XX means female. Forgetting to check pair 23 for the sex is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain the difference between trisomy and monosomy. Give the total number of chromosomes for each and one example.
